content.text: Flutter doesn't turn your widgets into Android or iOS controls. Its framework lays out and paints the whole UI, its engine rasterizes the result (with Impeller on iOS and modern Android), and the operating system only lends it a surface, input and accessibility services. That's why a
looks the same everywhere until you ask for the adaptive one, and why embedding a real native view has a price.

Two days before release, the iOS tester attaches a screenshot to a ticket: "The notifications toggle on iPhone looks like Android." The developer who built the screen is sure it's a Flutter bug, because
on iOS. It never was. On the iPhone, that toggle is exactly what it is on a Pixel: shapes Flutter painted itself, with no native switch anywhere in the app.
The belief goes like this: Flutter is a translation layer. You write
, and at runtime Flutter maps each widget to the platform's own control, a
on iOS and an Android switch on Android. The OS draws your UI; Flutter only tells it what to show.

It's a reasonable guess. Flutter's own architecture overview notes that cross-platform frameworks typically work exactly that way, as a layer over the native Android and iOS UI libraries. Flutter apps are called native too, and in release they really are compiled to machine code. On an iPhone, a Flutter app scrolls with iOS physics and uses the San Francisco font, so it feels like iOS did the work. And you can embed real native views. All true, and none of it makes your widgets native controls.

In the docs' words, Flutter "has its own implementations of each UI control, rather than deferring to those provided by the system". The OS gives Flutter a place to draw and forwards touches, keys and accessibility requests. Everything inside that rectangle is Flutter's work.
Flutter is built as layers, each depending on the one below it:

items.text: Framework
(Dart): widgets, layout, painting, gestures, and the Material and Cupertino libraries. This is the code you write against.
Engine
(mostly C++): the Dart runtime, text layout and the renderer that rasterizes every frame. The framework talks to it through
dart:ui
Embedder
(one per platform): starts the app, sets up threads, hands the engine a rendering surface and connects it to the OS for input and accessibility.

content.text: On Android, the whole Flutter UI of a typical app is displayed by one
, which the engine paints into a
. Your hundred widgets aren't a hundred Android views. They're pixels in one.
When a frame is needed, the framework builds your widgets into elements, creates or updates the render objects behind them, lays those out, and calls their
methods. The result is a scene of drawing commands, not a set of views. The engine then rasterizes that scene on the GPU with
, which precompiles its shaders when the engine itself is built, so they don't compile while your app runs.
Which renderer runs depends on the platform, and the docs are precise about it:

items.text: iOS
: Impeller is the only supported renderer, with no way to switch back to Skia.
Android
: Impeller is the default on API 29 and later. On older versions, or devices without Vulkan, it falls back to the legacy OpenGL renderer.
macOS, Windows and Linux
: Impeller is enabled by default as of Flutter 3.47.
Web
: Flutter uses Skia today.

content.text: "Native" means native code, not native widgets
In release builds, your Dart code is compiled to ARM or x64 machine code, so "native" is fair when it comes to speed. Platform APIs like the camera are reached through a

that calls Kotlin or Swift code, which is how most plugins work. The iOS feel is Flutter's work too: it reimplements page transitions, scroll physics, fonts and text selection, and adapts them to the platform automatically. Which control to show, though, is a design decision, and that one is yours.
Why the toggle looked like Android
is a Material widget, and it paints a Material switch on every platform. If you want each platform's convention, you have to ask for it:

content.text: checks the theme's platform: on iOS and macOS it looks and feels like the iOS control, elsewhere it's the Material one. Both are drawn by Flutter. The Cupertino library implements the iOS design language with Flutter's own widgets; it isn't a bridge to UIKit.

blocks.title: Preview the iOS look on an Android emulator

content.text: Because both looks are just Flutter pixels, setting
in a debug build makes adaptive widgets paint their iOS variant on Android. Fonts fall back, since San Francisco isn't available there, so keep a final check on a real iPhone.
When you really need a native view
Some UI is impractical to rebuild: a map SDK, a web view, a native ad. For those, Flutter has
embed a real native view inside the Flutter UI.

blocks.title: A native view inside Flutter is never free

content.text: The native view and Flutter's scene have to be kept in sync, and the docs say that overhead is why platform views are best kept for complex controls like maps. On Android, the default texture-layer mode can jank during fast scrolling and breaks accessibility for

s. Hybrid composition gives full native fidelity but merges the raster thread into the platform thread, which can lower the app's frame rate. The newer HCPP mode is experimental since Flutter 3.44 and needs Android API 34+, Vulkan and Impeller.

paints an iOS-style one on iOS and macOS
Flutter paints a scene, and the engine rasterizes it into a surface the embedder provides
It means machine code in release, plus platform channels for native APIs
An iOS feel needs iOS controls

Native views mix in for free

content.text: How to apply it in your project

items.title: Choose a look per control, on purpose

content.text: Decide between Material everywhere, Cupertino everywhere, or
constructors. For input controls like switches, sliders and dialogs, the docs recommend following each platform's conventions, which

items.title: Review both platforms from the first screen

content.text: Don't assume a widget will "look native" on its own. Check every new screen on an iPhone and an Android phone, or at least with the

items.title: Reach for plugins before platform views

content.text: Camera, location and payments are platform APIs, not UI: a plugin reaches them through platform channels, no native view needed. Embed a native view only when the UI itself can't be rebuilt, then profile scrolling on a low-end Android phone.

items.title: Isolate rendering bugs before reporting them

content.text: If something renders wrong on Android, run
once. If the glitch disappears, it's tied to the renderer, and that's exactly what to put in the bug report.

items.text: Flutter doesn't map widgets to native controls: its framework paints the whole UI and the engine rasterizes it.
Impeller renders on iOS and on Android API 29+ (older or non-Vulkan devices fall back to OpenGL); the web uses Skia.
"Native" refers to compiled machine code and to platform channels, not to the widgets you see.
A platform's look is your choice: Material, Cupertino or
.adaptive
, all drawn by Flutter.
Use platform views only for native UI you can't reasonably rebuild, and measure what they cost.
